html:
Perry's expedition was the arrival of US Navy warships in Japan in 1853 and 1854, under Commodore Matthew C. Perry, which forced the Tokugawa shogunate to open the country to foreign trade after more than two centuries of strict seclusion.

Since the 1630s Japan had kept foreigners out. Only Dutch and Chinese traders were allowed, at Nagasaki, the Dutch confined to the small island of Dejima. By the 1850s the United States wanted Japanese ports for its whaling ships and for steamships crossing the Pacific to China, where Britain had just forced open trade in the First Opium War.

In July 1853 Perry sailed into Edo Bay with four ships, two of them coal-fired steamers belching smoke. The Japanese called them the "black ships". He refused to go to Nagasaki and delivered a letter from President Fillmore, promising to return for an answer. He came back in early 1854 with a larger fleet. Facing guns they could not match, the shogun's officials signed the Convention of Kanagawa, opening two ports and allowing a US consul.

Britain, Russia and the Netherlands soon won similar deals, and later "unequal treaties" gave foreigners special rights. The shogunate's weakness in the face of the West discredited it. Within fifteen years it fell, and the Meiji Restoration of 1868 put Japan on a crash course of modernisation. The black ships became, in Japanese memory, the moment the modern world arrived.
sum: Perry's expedition was the arrival of US Navy warships in Japan in 1853 and 1854, under Commodore Matthew C. Perry, which forced the Tokugawa shogunate to open the country to foreign trade after more than two centuries of strict seclusion.
